newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - April 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - April 27.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
SUNDAY TELEGRAPH
-- TUCKEY LOOKS AT TWO BILLION STG SPLIT FOR MEPC

Property company MEPC has begun radical restructuring to try to ease shareholder dissent and prevent a hostile bid. The programme will be called Project Performance, and has been instigated by chief executive James Tuckey. The move could lead to a breakup of the two billion stg company.
-- REGAN'S GALILEO DOOMED TO SELF-DESTRUCT

The vehicle set up by Andrew Regan for his takeover attempt on the businesses of the Co-operative Wholesale Society, Galileo, is to go into voluntary liquidation. This follows speculation that its shareholders have limited payments to key advisers to a minimum.
-- HOLLICK LETTER SHUNNED

Chief executive of United News & Media, Lord Hollick, is trying to gain support among other business leaders for an open letter condemning the Conservative government and backing Labour. It is uncertain whether he has managed to win substantial backing, apart from businessmen who have already declared their support for Labour.
-- BERKELEY SQUARE CONCERT PARTY

Concert, the 12.5 billion stg merged business between British Telecom and America's MCI, is to set up its headquarters in London's West End, paying Britain's highest office rent in six years. The company is in negotiations with Prudential to occupy the development in Berkeley Square.
-- EQUITY & LAW RESHAPES AFTER SALE FALLS THROUGH

Equity & Law is planning radical restructuring and a new business plan to improve its prospects of finding a buyer. The company is to accelerate compensation for pension mis-selling victims and has set aside 32 million stg for this. Staff will be told about new employment contracts, reduced overtime and longer working days.
SUNDAY TIMES
-- TAXES 'NEED TO RISE SHARPLY' TO CURB BORROWING

The National Institute of Economic and Social Research warns that big tax rises will be needed to control public borrowing even if public spending is kept on a tight rein. They claim that Britain has an underlying budget deficit of 2.5 percent of gross domestic product.
-- REGAN FACES FULL INSIDER DEALS PROBE

Andrew Regan faces the prospect of a full-blown insider- dealing inquiry by the Stock Exchange into Lanica Trust shares. The exchange will examine high volumes of dealings in Lanica between September, when Regan first bought into the company, and January, when shares hit a high of 20.50 stg.
-- DAEWOO PLANS 200 MILLION STG BRITISH ENGINE PLANT

According to motor-industry executives, Korean car maker Daewoo is planning to build a 200 million stg engine factory in the West Midlands. The plant will be a stepping stone to an eventual car-assembly operation that will supply the West European market.
-- BRITAIN'S 'THIN CAT' BOSSES

According to a survey from PE International, the management consultants, directors of Britain's small firms are Europe's 'thin cats', earning far less than their continental counterparts. Similar differences exist for finance directors, sales directors and heads of manufacturing.
-- SPORTS DIVISION IN RUNNING FOR FLOAT

Tom Hunter, the entrepreneur behind Sports Division, Europe's top sports-clothing retailer, is considering floating the company. He could emerge as one of Britain's wealthiest retailers, with a stock market value of more than 200 million stg.
THE OBSERVER
-- CO-OP SACKS ITS TREACHEROUS DUO

Co-op executives accused of leaking highly sensitive documents to Andrew Regan, Allan Green and David Chambers, have been sacked. Roger Jones, secretary of the Co-operative Wholesale Society, accused them of betraying the company, colleagues and staff.
-- FRANCE BEATS UK IN INVESTMENT STAKES

According to a study from the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, Britain has been overtaken by France as the prime European destination for inward investment. The study also reveals that the biggest slice of that investment comes from Britain. This will embarrass John Major, who last week criticised France's federalist social and economic policies.
-- LONDON ELECTRICITY OFFERS 'ILLEGAL' DEBT RECOVERY SERVICE

London Electricity has been accused by the Data Protection Registrar of illegally using customer information to run a debt recovery service for local authorities. The company was tracing debts from its own customers through its subsidiary Knight Debt Recovery Services and began to offer the service to councils in London.
-- KINGFISHER AT ODDS WITH LITTLEWOODS OVER PRICE OF STORES

Negotiations between Kingfisher and Littlewoods High Street Stores are close to collapse. Kingfisher accuses Littlewoods of not being clear about what is on offer and is expecting too high a price. Kingfisher has offered 500 million stg for the chain, however Littlewoods wants 600 million stg.
-- PROCTER & GAMBLE URGE SAATCHI MARRIAGE

Procter & Gamble, the household goods multinational, is thought to be urging a partnership between a newly independent Saatchi and Saatchi and US-based DMB&B, another of its favoured international advertising agencies. P&G is Saatchi and Saatchi's largest international client.
INDEPENDENT ON SUNDAY
-- CO-OP PLANS HUGE OVERHAUL

Following the aborted bid by Andrew Regan, the Co-operative movement is planning a massive overhaul to improve profitability and restore some direction to the organisation. The CWS is anxious to conclude a five-month strategic review of its operations to head off a more credible bidder and pacify the growing number of its managers who are looking for more radical solutions.
-- VIRGIN ASKS ANGEL TO GET IT ROLLING

Virgin Rail is in discussions with privatised rail leasing company Angel with a view to win the country's biggest ever rolling stock order. Angel will be invited to join a dedicated rail procurement team that Virgin is establishing in readiness for an 800 million stg order to refit its fleets servicing the West Coast main line and Cross Country franchises.
-- MOBILE PHONES HEAD PARADE OF PRIVATE STARS

The top four placings in the Independent's 100 listing of Britain's fastest growing companies have been won by the mobile phones market. The top three companies, European Telecom, Anglia Telecom Centres and Mobile Systems International, achieved annual sales growth of more than 100 percent over five years.
-- REBEL THREAT TO INTERFLORA

Plans by Interflora to convert to limited company status and possibly float on the Stock Exchange has led to more than 400 dissident florists, led by Leeds florist Beverley Wood, seeking to throw out the company's entire board of directors. The dissidents are also angry over a proposed six-fold increase in the annual membership fee.
-- INDUSTRY DIGS IN ON WINDFALL TAX

Privatised industries are preparing plans to counter any threat by a Labour government to extend its windfall tax into a more permanent tax on excess profits. There has been speculation, fuelled by the absence of any precise detail on how much would be raised from which companies and on what basis, that the tax will be extended into an annual charge.
MAIL ON SUNDAY
-- SWISS BANK RUNS A RULER OVER CO-OP

Credit Suisse First Boston is considering a bid for the Co-operative Wholesale Society. The group is one of a number of banks assessing the Co-op on behalf of clients. CSFB does not see the complicated structure of the Co-op as an insurmountable problem. It is also believed that Allied Irish Bank is considering a bid.
-- TOUGH BA SET FOR STRIKE SHOWDOWN

BASSA, part of the Transport and General Workers Union, has warned it will hold a strike ballot unless British Airways negotiates with them. However, chief executive Bob Ayling says there is nothing to discuss. BA wants to cut costs by one billion stg over three years and is prepared to improve pay and pensions in return for more efficiency.
-- IMRO CHIEF ACCUSES THE 'SOFT' WATCHDOGS

Chief executive of the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation, Phillip Thorpe, has attacked other watchdogs for being too "soft". He warned that Labour Party plans for a single regulator could hurt investors because standards are likely to be dragged down.
-- IRISH EYES ON FOUR BILLION STG SOCIETY FLOTATION

First National, Ireland's largest building society, is preparing a four billion stg stock market floatation. ABN Amro, the City merchant banker, is advising. Operations director Gerry Murphy could not confirm or deny the reports. The society has just acquired The Mortgage Corporation, a Salomon Brothers subsidiary with assets of 1.3 billion stg.
